screens.title: Interrupts and Real-Time Response
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore interrupts, the hardware mechanism that lets a processor stop its current work and handle an urgent event right away. You will learn what an interrupt is, why it is a better choice than tight polling for many events, and how the ARM Cortex-M uses the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller to prioritize and nest handlers. We'll use a concrete example from a LaunchPad board: configuring a falling-edge interrupt on a GPIO pin so a button press increments a counter and toggles an LED. I will explain the four steps you must perform to enable an interrupt: enable the peripheral, enable the NVIC entry, set or accept a priority, and provide a correctly named ISR that clears the flag. We'll also compare polling and interrupts in terms of C P U usage, responsiveness, and complexity, and highlight a common trap: failing to clear the interrupt flag causes the interrupt to fire repeatedly. By the end of this chapter you will understand why interrupts are essential for real-time response, how to configure and write a basic ISR, and when polling remains the simpler, acceptable choice.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Interrupts and Real-Time Response
Interrupts and Real-Time Response
Learn how hardware signals and the NVIC let a microcontroller respond immediately and efficiently.
Interrupts let the CPU suspend the main program to run a short handler for urgent events. This reduces wasted cycles from polling and enables sleeping until work arrives. You'll see how the NVIC manages priority and nesting so critical events preempt lower-priority handlers.
In this lesson
Configure NVIC, write an ISR, and compare polling vs interrupts
Concrete example: falling-edge interrupt on PF4 to count button presses. We'll show the config steps, a sample ISR, and the common pitfalls to avoid.

What an interrupt is and how it yields real-time reaction.
NVIC & Priority
How the Cortex-M organizes many interrupt lines and priorities for nesting.
ISR Best Practices
The essential do's and don'ts when writing handlers and clearing flags.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
LaunchPad demo
PF4 falling-edge triggers ISR that increments a volatile counter.
Timing idea
Main loop sleeps or polls slowly. When the button fires, CPU saves registers, jumps to ISR, clears the flag, and returns. This minimizes latency compared with frequent polling.
Why start here?
Understanding interrupts is foundational when you build responsive embedded systems that must react to external events without wasting CPU time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently explain what an interrupt is, configure the ARM Cortex-M NVIC for an external event, write a working interrupt service routine for a GPIO pin, and weigh the trade-offs between polling and interrupts for different tasks. Each objective focuses on practical competence: you will not only name parts of the NVIC but enable an interrupt and set its priority. You will write an ISR that clears its flag and modifies a volatile counter safely. Finally, you will learn when polling is adequate and when interrupts are preferable, using examples like periodic timer ticks versus rare but urgent events such as a user button or an emergency stop. These skills let you design responsive, power-efficient embedded programs and avoid common pitfalls that cause runaway interrupts or missed deadlines.

screens.title: Polling vs. Interrupts
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by contrasting polling and interrupts with real examples you already know. Polling means the main loop repeatedly asks a peripheral if something happened. For example, a loop that checks a switch state every millisecond is polling. It is easy to write and predictable, but if the event is rare the C P U spends most of its time checking empty conditions. Interrupts invert this model: hardware signals the processor when the event occurs, and the processor runs a brief handler immediately. A concrete example is a door sensor that rarely changes; polling wastes cycles, whereas an interrupt wakes the C P U only when needed. A common misconception is to assume interrupts always complicate code; they do add complexity in configuration and concurrency, but they also allow the processor to sleep and conserve power and provide much lower latency. Another contrast: if an event is periodic and frequent, like a fast timer tick used for scheduling, simple polling or tight timer-driven loops can be adequate because handler overhead and context switching may outweigh benefits. Key takeaway: choose polling when events are frequent and predictable, choose interrupts when events are rare or time-critical.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Polling vs. Interrupts
Polling
The CPU repeatedly checks a condition in the main loop. It is straightforward and predictable but can waste cycles.
Example
A loop checking a button state every millisecond.
Common mistake
Polling for rare events wastes CPU and increases power consumption.
Interrupts
The hardware signals the CPU and execution jumps to an ISR. This provides low latency and lets the CPU sleep when idle.
Example
A button press triggers a falling-edge interrupt and the ISR increments a counter immediately.
Key benefit
Lower latency and reduced idle CPU work; suitable for rare, urgent signals.
Decision mnemonic
Frequency × Urgency
High frequency → polling acceptable. High urgency → interrupts preferred.
Misconception check
Interrupts are always better
Not always: for simple, frequent tasks the overhead of context switching can outweigh benefits.
Try this
Measure both versions
Implement polling and interrupt versions and compare CPU activity and latency.

screens.title: What is an Interrupt?
screens.narratorSegment: An interrupt is a hardware signal that causes the processor to suspend its current execution and run a predefined routine to handle that event. Concretely, when an interrupt arrives the C P U saves a minimal context—registers and program counter—then looks up the handler address in the vector table and jumps to that function, called the Interrupt Service Routine or ISR. After the ISR completes and the interrupt flag is cleared, the C P U restores the saved context and resumes the interrupted code as if nothing happened. A clear example is a GPIO falling-edge: the GPIO peripheral sets a flag and the NVIC signals the C P U; the ISR runs, clears the flag in the GPIOICR register, increments a volatile counter, and returns. A common misconception is that an ISR is just another function; it is not: ISRs must be short, must clear flags, and must respect priority and nesting rules. Takeaway: interrupt handling is a brief, atomic response path that lets the system react immediately to hardware events without busy-waiting. What is an Interrupt? means interrupt arrives → cpu saves state → vector lookup → isr executes → clear flag → restore state and continue.. In practical terms, a concise definition and the processor's response sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › What is an Interrupt?
Definition
A hardware event that causes the CPU to pause execution and run a short handler immediately.
Sequence
  1. Interrupt signal asserted by peripheral
  2. CPU saves state and vectors to ISR
  3. ISR services event and clears flag
  4. CPU restores state and resumes
Concrete example
A falling-edge on PF4 sets GPIO flag; NVIC directs CPU to GPIOF_Handler which increments a volatile counter and clears GPIOICR.
Analogy
A fire alarm
The alarm interrupts normal activity and demands a short, urgent response; once handled and silenced, regular activities resume.
Key Takeaway

An ISR is a short, prioritized response routine; it must clear its flag and return quickly so other interrupts can be serviced.

screens.title: NVIC and Priority on Cortex-M
screens.narratorSegment: The ARM Cortex-M microcontroller uses the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller, or NVIC, to manage many sources of interrupts with priority and nesting. The NVIC can support up to 240 interrupt lines and typically uses a limited set of priority levels; the Cortex-M4F commonly exposes 16 priority levels. Each enabled interrupt has an entry in the NVIC so the controller can mask, enable, or set priority. Nesting means that while an ISR runs, a higher-priority interrupt can preempt it; the NVIC saves the current context and vectors to the higher-priority handler. This mechanism is critical for systems where some events, like an emergency stop, must always interrupt less-critical handlers such as user-interface updates. The configuration you perform sets the NVIC enable bit for a given interrupt number and optionally writes a priority field. Remember: lower numerical value means higher priority on many Cortex-M implementations. This detail determines which ISR can preempt another and should match your system's urgency model. NVIC and Priority on Cortex-M means nvic enables, ranks, and nests interrupts so higher-priority events can preempt lower-priority handlers for real-time guarantees.. In practical terms, how nested vectored interrupt controller organizes interrupts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › NVIC and Priority
NVIC concept
A hardware controller that enables, prioritizes, and allows nesting of up to many interrupt sources on Cortex-M devices.
Priority behavior
Lower numerical priority value indicates higher priority. A higher-priority interrupt can preempt a lower-priority ISR.
Nesting example
If an ISR for a sensor runs at priority 5 and an emergency stop at priority 1 fires, the emergency ISR interrupts the sensor ISR to handle the urgent event.
NVIC registers
EN, PRI and grouping
Write NVIC_EN0 to enable an interrupt number and NVIC_PRIx to set priority bits for that interrupt.
Pro tip
Plan priorities based on urgency; reserve the highest priorities for critical safety events to prevent missed deadlines.

screens.title: Configuring an Interrupt
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring an interrupt requires a clear sequence so the controller and peripheral are ready and safe. Follow these four steps: first, enable the interrupt in the peripheral itself — for GPIO, enable the pin's interrupt mask so the port can signal an event. Second, enable the corresponding interrupt in the NVIC so the C P U will accept vectors from that source, often by writing a bit in NVIC_EN registers using the interrupt number. Third, set the interrupt priority if your system needs differentiated urgency; lower numeric values often represent higher priority. Fourth, write the ISR with the exact name expected by the vector table and ensure the ISR clears the interrupt flag in the peripheral's interrupt-clear register. A concrete example is setting up PF4: clear and configure edge triggers, clear any pending flag, enable the mask, and then set NVIC_EN0_R with 1 shifted by 30 for interrupt number 30. Misconfiguration order matters — enabling NVIC before the peripheral mask can cause spurious interrupts. Takeaway: follow the sequence to avoid unexpected immediate triggers. Configuring an Interrupt means enable peripheral interrupt, enable nvic, set priority, implement isr that clears interrupt flag.. In practical terms, the four essential steps to enable a peripheral interrupt. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Configuring an Interrupt
Configuration steps
1
Enable peripheral
Enable the GPIO pin interrupt mask and set edge/level trigger registers appropriately.
2
Enable NVIC
Write the NVIC enable register for the interrupt number so CPU receives vectors.
3
Set priority
Set the NVIC priority field so critical events preempt less-critical ones.

Write ISR
Provide the correctly named ISR and clear the peripheral interrupt flag before returning.
Order matters
Enable peripheral configuration and clear pending flags before enabling NVIC to avoid spurious early interrupts.
Pitfall
If you enable NVIC while a peripheral flag is set, the ISR may run immediately. Clear flags first.

screens.title: GPIO Interrupt Example: PF4
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided GPIO example that configures a falling-edge interrupt on Port F pin 4, commonly the user button on a LaunchPad. The code defines volatile switchCount so that both main code and the ISR see changes. The ISR is named GPIOF_Handler because the vector table contains the address for interrupt 30, which maps to Port F. Inside the handler we check the RIS register to confirm PF4 caused the interrupt, increment the counter, and then write to GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R to clear the flag. The init function first disables the PF4 mask while configuring edge sensitivity registers: IS for edge-sensitive, IBE to disable both-edges, and IEV to select falling edge. It explicitly clears any pending interrupt, sets the mask, and enables NVIC by setting the appropriate bit in NVIC_EN0_R and writes a priority into NVIC_PRI7_R. A common mistake is not clearing GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R; leaving the flag set causes the interrupt to fire immediately after returning, typically creating an infinite loop. Practice reading these registers to see the effect of each step. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › GPIO Interrupt Example
Key registers in the example
  • GPIO_PORTF_IS_R: selects edge or level sensitivity
  • GPIO_PORTF_IBE_R: enables both-edge triggers
  • GPIO_PORTF_IEV_R: selects rising or falling edge
  • GPIO_PORTF_IM_R: interrupt mask for pins
  • GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R: interrupt clear register
  • NVIC_EN0_R and NVIC_PRI7_R: NVIC enable and priority registers
// core of example (visual only)
volatile uint32_t switchCount = 0;

void GPIOF_Handler(void) {
    if (GPIO_PORTF_RIS_R & 0x10) {
        switchCount++;
        GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R |= 0x10; // clear PF4
    }
}

void GPIOF_InitInterrupt(void) {
    GPIO_PORTF_IM_R &= ~0x10; // disable before configure
    GPIO_PORTF_IS_R &= ~0x10; // edge-sensitive
    GPIO_PORTF_IBE_R &= ~0x10; // not both edges
    GPIO_PORTF_IEV_R &= ~0x10; // falling edge
    GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R |= 0x10;  // clear any prior flag
    GPIO_PORTF_IM_R |= 0x10;   // enable interrupt mask
    NVIC_EN0_R |= (1 << 30);   // enable in NVIC
    NVIC_PRI7_R = (NVIC_PRI7_R & 0xFF00FFFF) | 0x00A00000; // set priority
}
Explanation highlights
The ISR checks the raw interrupt status to confirm the cause, updates program state using a volatile variable, and clears the flag to avoid retriggering. The init sequence prevents spurious interrupts by clearing pending flags before enabling NVIC.
Pitfall
Failing to clear GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R causes the ISR to fire immediately in a loop.

screens.title: Vector Table and ISR Naming
screens.narratorSegment: On ARM Cortex-M devices the vector table is a table of function pointers stored at the beginning of flash. Each interrupt number has a corresponding entry that points to the ISR for that source. The toolchain and startup code expect specific names for handlers because those names are placed into the table or referenced by weak symbols that the linker overrides. In the example the Port F interrupt is interrupt number 30 and the table entry points to GPIOF_Handler. If your ISR has the wrong name or signature, the default handler will run instead or the program may fault. A frequent misconception is that you can name ISRs arbitrarily; in practice you must match the name or change the vector table entry explicitly. Another practical point: the vector table is consulted after the C P U has saved the minimal context; therefore the name and address must be valid and accessible from flash during exceptions. Takeaway: use the correct ISR name or update the vector table so your handler is invoked correctly. Vector Table and ISR Naming means the vector table maps an interrupt number to an isr address; isr names must match the table entries or be linked accordingly.. In practical terms, why isr names and the vector table must match. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ISR naming

screens.title: Clearing Interrupt Flags
screens.narratorSegment: After servicing an interrupt the ISR must explicitly clear the peripheral's interrupt flag so the event is considered handled. For GPIO on Cortex-M devices this means writing the pin bit to the interrupt clear register, for example GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R |= 0x10 to clear PF4. If the ISR does not clear the flag the hardware still sees the event as pending and reasserts the interrupt, which typically causes the C P U to re-enter the ISR immediately, producing an infinite loop of interrupts that prevents normal program progress. A common misunderstanding is to assume returning from an ISR implicitly clears hardware flags; it does not. Clearing must be done by writing to the peripheral's clear register, and the write must happen before returning. Sometimes you also need to clear both software and hardware flags or to debounce mechanical buttons to avoid repeated triggers from contact bounce. Takeaway: always identify and clear the correct flag bits inside the ISR before returning to avoid interrupt storms. Module 07 › Chapter 7.2 › Clearing Interrupt Flags
Why clear flags?
Clearing the hardware flag tells the peripheral the event has been handled; otherwise the interrupt remains pending and will retrigger.
Example action
Write GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R |= 0x10 to clear PF4 in the ISR before returning.
Misconception
Returning from the ISR does not clear peripheral flags automatically; explicit clearing is required.
Danger
If you forget to clear a flag, the CPU may become stuck servicing the same interrupt repeatedly.
Tip
Clear flags early in the ISR, then perform minimal state updates, and always keep handlers short.

screens.title: ISR Best Practices and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Interrupt Service Routines must be short, deterministic, and safe with shared data. Keep ISRs minimal: clear the flag, update a volatile variable or set a simple event flag, and return. In the example the ISR increments a volatile counter and toggles an LED; marking the counter volatile ensures the main code and ISR see the same value. Avoid long-running operations such as delays or blocking calls inside an ISR because they prevent other interrupts from running and can miss higher-priority deadlines. The chapter warns specifically that using delay inside an ISR is dangerous for this reason. Also be careful with shared data: if the main code reads or writes a multi-byte value updated in an ISR, you may need to disable interrupts briefly around the access or use atomic techniques. A common misconception is that volatile alone solves all concurrency issues; volatile ensures visibility but not atomicity. Takeaway: make ISRs short, clear flags, use volatile for visibility, avoid blocking code, and plan for atomic access when sharing data. Principles
  • Clear the hardware flag immediately.
  • Keep handlers short and non-blocking.
  • Use volatile for variables shared with main code.
  • Avoid delays or heavy processing inside ISR.
Concrete example
ISR increments volatile switchCount and toggles LED. Heavy logging or delays should be done in the main loop instead, triggered by a flag set in the ISR.

Practical tip

screens.title: When to Use Interrupts in Real Systems
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding to use interrupts depends on the event frequency, urgency, and system complexity. Use interrupts for rare but time-sensitive signals like user button presses, emergency stops, or asynchronous peripheral input that require immediate attention. For instance, an emergency stop that must stop motors should be assigned a high NVIC priority so it preempts other handlers. For frequent, periodic events such as a stable timer tick used for scheduler ticks, polling or timer-driven callbacks can be simpler and more predictable because the C P U knows when the event will occur. Another practical consideration is power: interrupts allow the C P U to sleep and wake only when needed, reducing energy consumption. Also think about debouncing mechanical inputs; even with interrupts you may need simple debouncing logic or to handle multiple transitions. Finally, remember that interrupts add complexity in concurrency and testing, so reserve them for when their benefits in latency or power outweigh that complexity. Question to reflect: for your current project which signals are rare and urgent enough to justify an interrupt? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore interrupts, the hardware mechanism that lets a processor stop its current work and handle an urgent event right away. You will learn what an interrupt is, why it is a better choice than tight polling for many events, and how the ARM Cortex-M uses the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller to prioritize and nest handlers. We'll use a concrete example from a LaunchPad board: configuring a falling-edge interrupt on a GPIO pin so a button press increments a counter and toggles an LED. I will explain the four steps you must perform to enable an interrupt: enable the peripheral, enable the NVIC entry, set or accept a priority, and provide a correctly named ISR that clears the flag. We'll also compare polling and interrupts in terms of C P U usage, responsiveness, and complexity, and highlight a common trap: failing to clear the interrupt flag causes the interrupt to fire repeatedly. By the end of this chapter you will understand why interrupts are essential for real-time response, how to configure and write a basic ISR, and when polling remains the simpler, acceptable choice.

By the end of this chapter you will confidently explain what an interrupt is, configure the ARM Cortex-M NVIC for an external event, write a working interrupt service routine for a GPIO pin, and weigh the trade-offs between polling and interrupts for different tasks. Each objective focuses on practical competence: you will not only name parts of the NVIC but enable an interrupt and set its priority. You will write an ISR that clears its flag and modifies a volatile counter safely. Finally, you will learn when polling is adequate and when interrupts are preferable, using examples like periodic timer ticks versus rare but urgent events such as a user button or an emergency stop. These skills let you design responsive, power-efficient embedded programs and avoid common pitfalls that cause runaway interrupts or missed deadlines.

In addition to conceptual goals, this chapter includes a hands-on activity and an assessment idea so you can practice and verify understanding. The lab asks you to use PF4 on a LaunchPad to count button presses with an interrupt while the main loop sleeps. Your ISR should increment a volatile counter and toggle an LED. Then use the UART to print the count every five seconds and compare C P U usage to a polling version. The assessment checks two misunderstandings: forgetting to clear the interrupt flag, which causes re-triggering and a potential interrupt storm, and doing delays inside an ISR, which blocks other interrupts and misses deadlines. These practice steps tie the configuration, ISR writing, and trade-off evaluation into a single, verifiable exercise. Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment means implement pf4 interrupt-driven counting, report via uart, and compare power/cpu to a polling baseline.. In practical terms, what you'll build and how you will be tested. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Begin by contrasting polling and interrupts with real examples you already know. Polling means the main loop repeatedly asks a peripheral if something happened. For example, a loop that checks a switch state every millisecond is polling. It is easy to write and predictable, but if the event is rare the C P U spends most of its time checking empty conditions. Interrupts invert this model: hardware signals the processor when the event occurs, and the processor runs a brief handler immediately. A concrete example is a door sensor that rarely changes; polling wastes cycles, whereas an interrupt wakes the C P U only when needed. A common misconception is to assume interrupts always complicate code; they do add complexity in configuration and concurrency, but they also allow the processor to sleep and conserve power and provide much lower latency. Another contrast: if an event is periodic and frequent, like a fast timer tick used for scheduling, simple polling or tight timer-driven loops can be adequate because handler overhead and context switching may outweigh benefits. Key takeaway: choose polling when events are frequent and predictable, choose interrupts when events are rare or time-critical.

An interrupt is a hardware signal that causes the processor to suspend its current execution and run a predefined routine to handle that event. Concretely, when an interrupt arrives the C P U saves a minimal context—registers and program counter—then looks up the handler address in the vector table and jumps to that function, called the Interrupt Service Routine or ISR. After the ISR completes and the interrupt flag is cleared, the C P U restores the saved context and resumes the interrupted code as if nothing happened. A clear example is a GPIO falling-edge: the GPIO peripheral sets a flag and the NVIC signals the C P U; the ISR runs, clears the flag in the GPIOICR register, increments a volatile counter, and returns. A common misconception is that an ISR is just another function; it is not: ISRs must be short, must clear flags, and must respect priority and nesting rules. Takeaway: interrupt handling is a brief, atomic response path that lets the system react immediately to hardware events without busy-waiting. What is an Interrupt? means interrupt arrives → cpu saves state → vector lookup → isr executes → clear flag → restore state and continue.. In practical terms, a concise definition and the processor's response sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The ARM Cortex-M microcontroller uses the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller, or NVIC, to manage many sources of interrupts with priority and nesting. The NVIC can support up to 240 interrupt lines and typically uses a limited set of priority levels; the Cortex-M4F commonly exposes 16 priority levels. Each enabled interrupt has an entry in the NVIC so the controller can mask, enable, or set priority. Nesting means that while an ISR runs, a higher-priority interrupt can preempt it; the NVIC saves the current context and vectors to the higher-priority handler. This mechanism is critical for systems where some events, like an emergency stop, must always interrupt less-critical handlers such as user-interface updates. The configuration you perform sets the NVIC enable bit for a given interrupt number and optionally writes a priority field. Remember: lower numerical value means higher priority on many Cortex-M implementations. This detail determines which ISR can preempt another and should match your system's urgency model. NVIC and Priority on Cortex-M means nvic enables, ranks, and nests interrupts so higher-priority events can preempt lower-priority handlers for real-time guarantees.. In practical terms, how nested vectored interrupt controller organizes interrupts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuring an interrupt requires a clear sequence so the controller and peripheral are ready and safe. Follow these four steps: first, enable the interrupt in the peripheral itself — for GPIO, enable the pin's interrupt mask so the port can signal an event. Second, enable the corresponding interrupt in the NVIC so the C P U will accept vectors from that source, often by writing a bit in NVIC_EN registers using the interrupt number. Third, set the interrupt priority if your system needs differentiated urgency; lower numeric values often represent higher priority. Fourth, write the ISR with the exact name expected by the vector table and ensure the ISR clears the interrupt flag in the peripheral's interrupt-clear register. A concrete example is setting up PF4: clear and configure edge triggers, clear any pending flag, enable the mask, and then set NVIC_EN0_R with 1 shifted by 30 for interrupt number 30. Misconfiguration order matters — enabling NVIC before the peripheral mask can cause spurious interrupts. Takeaway: follow the sequence to avoid unexpected immediate triggers. Configuring an Interrupt means enable peripheral interrupt, enable nvic, set priority, implement isr that clears interrupt flag.. In practical terms, the four essential steps to enable a peripheral interrupt. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the provided GPIO example that configures a falling-edge interrupt on Port F pin 4, commonly the user button on a LaunchPad. The code defines volatile switchCount so that both main code and the ISR see changes. The ISR is named GPIOF_Handler because the vector table contains the address for interrupt 30, which maps to Port F. Inside the handler we check the RIS register to confirm PF4 caused the interrupt, increment the counter, and then write to GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R to clear the flag. The init function first disables the PF4 mask while configuring edge sensitivity registers: IS for edge-sensitive, IBE to disable both-edges, and IEV to select falling edge. It explicitly clears any pending interrupt, sets the mask, and enables NVIC by setting the appropriate bit in NVIC_EN0_R and writes a priority into NVIC_PRI7_R. A common mistake is not clearing GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R; leaving the flag set causes the interrupt to fire immediately after returning, typically creating an infinite loop. Practice reading these registers to see the effect of each step. In practical terms, walkthrough of the sample initialization and isr code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. On ARM Cortex-M devices the vector table is a table of function pointers stored at the beginning of flash. Each interrupt number has a corresponding entry that points to the ISR for that source. The toolchain and startup code expect specific names for handlers because those names are placed into the table or referenced by weak symbols that the linker overrides. In the example the Port F interrupt is interrupt number 30 and the table entry points to GPIOF_Handler. If your ISR has the wrong name or signature, the default handler will run instead or the program may fault. A frequent misconception is that you can name ISRs arbitrarily; in practice you must match the name or change the vector table entry explicitly. Another practical point: the vector table is consulted after the C P U has saved the minimal context; therefore the name and address must be valid and accessible from flash during exceptions. After servicing an interrupt the ISR must explicitly clear the peripheral's interrupt flag so the event is considered handled. For GPIO on Cortex-M devices this means writing the pin bit to the interrupt clear register, for example GPIO_PORTF_ICR_R |= 0x10 to clear PF4. If the ISR does not clear the flag the hardware still sees the event as pending and reasserts the interrupt, which typically causes the C P U to re-enter the ISR immediately, producing an infinite loop of interrupts that prevents normal program progress. A common misunderstanding is to assume returning from an ISR implicitly clears hardware flags; it does not. Clearing must be done by writing to the peripheral's clear register, and the write must happen before returning. Sometimes you also need to clear both software and hardware flags or to debounce mechanical buttons to avoid repeated triggers from contact bounce. Takeaway: always identify and clear the correct flag bits inside the ISR before returning to avoid interrupt storms. Interrupt Service Routines must be short, deterministic, and safe with shared data. Keep ISRs minimal: clear the flag, update a volatile variable or set a simple event flag, and return. In the example the ISR increments a volatile counter and toggles an LED; marking the counter volatile ensures the main code and ISR see the same value. Avoid long-running operations such as delays or blocking calls inside an ISR because they prevent other interrupts from running and can miss higher-priority deadlines. The chapter warns specifically that using delay inside an ISR is dangerous for this reason. Also be careful with shared data: if the main code reads or writes a multi-byte value updated in an ISR, you may need to disable interrupts briefly around the access or use atomic techniques. A common misconception is that volatile alone solves all concurrency issues; volatile ensures visibility but not atomicity. Deciding to use interrupts depends on the event frequency, urgency, and system complexity. Use interrupts for rare but time-sensitive signals like user button presses, emergency stops, or asynchronous peripheral input that require immediate attention. For instance, an emergency stop that must stop motors should be assigned a high NVIC priority so it preempts other handlers. For frequent, periodic events such as a stable timer tick used for scheduler ticks, polling or timer-driven callbacks can be simpler and more predictable because the C P U knows when the event will occur. Another practical consideration is power: interrupts allow the C P U to sleep and wake only when needed, reducing energy consumption. Also think about debouncing mechanical inputs; even with interrupts you may need simple debouncing logic or to handle multiple transitions. Finally, remember that interrupts add complexity in concurrency and testing, so reserve them for when their benefits in latency or power outweigh that complexity.
